column1: # G4 phase 2: relate(t?) -- the CHECKED, TYPED, LINK-SHAPED reference
# (sketch/capability-review/g4-identity-relations.md). A constraint on a
# string-valued field: the string must be a TREE ADDRESS, the addressed
# node must exist in the evaluation, and -- when `t` is given -- `t` is
# unified INTO the target. The field's own value stays the address
# string.
# This is the piece a plain reference cannot be. `$.a.b` resolves by
# CLONING its target into place, so the row `link-vs-plain-ref` below
# generates a full copy of the auth node where the author meant a name;
# `link-not-embedding`, one line different, generates the address.
# An address is a PATH and nothing else (ADR-014): `$.a.b` from the
# document root, `.b` from the link's own sibling scope. There is no
# second namespace, so a model can be instantiated more than once and
# each instance resolves its own relative links -- the row
# `relative-per-instance` is the case that decided it.
# Every expectation was obtained by the parity probe (AGENTS.md): both
# engines were run over this corpus and diffed before any row was
# written.
# Columns: name<TAB>mode<TAB>src<TAB>expect
link-not-embedding
link-vs-plain-ref
link-inside-a-node
link-inside-list
link-forward
link-many-to-one
link-to-a-hyphen-key
# `.b` reads the link's own SIBLING scope, and every further dot is one
# step up from there -- exactly the reduction a relative reference's
# `.` segments perform, so the two addressing forms agree.
# This is what makes a model REUSABLE. `relative-per-instance` is the
# case that removed the identity mark: two instances of one model, each
# with its own value and each resolving its internal link inside
# itself. Under a global name namespace the two instances were one
# entity and the second override was a contradiction.
relative-sibling
relative-one-up
relative-through-a-copy
relative-per-instance

# `relate(t)` does not merely TEST the target against `t`, it unifies `t`
# INTO it: referring to something as a Service makes it one, and if it
# cannot be, the conflict is an ordinary error, located at the target the
# template meets. Check-only
# semantics would be non-monotone -- true, then false as the target
# grows -- and the lattice guarantee is that more information never
# falsifies what has been observed.
flow-adds-to-target
flow-inside-a-node
flow-kind-constrains
flow-conflict
flow-conflict-msg
flow-two-refers
# A MEMBER'S FLOW IS PART OF THAT MEMBER. `relate(t)` asserts `t` on
# ANOTHER node, so it takes effect only where the output takes the
# alternative making it. Committing every alternative's flow put
# `t_A & t_B` on the target -- more constrained than either alternative
# allows, which no reading of `A | B` licenses. Here `k:1` refuses the
# second alternative, so only `{z:1}` may land.
flow-from-a-discarded-alternative-does-not-land
# The same, with the two alternatives asking for CONFLICTING types at
# one key: the surviving alternative's type lands and the discarded
# one's is not met against it (which used to leave the target's key
# nil, and the internal trial sentinel reached the user).
flow-discarded-alternative-does-not-conflict
# The surviving alternative still flows when it is the SECOND one.
flow-from-the-second-alternative-lands
# A SURVIVOR'S FLOW MEETS ANOTHER LINK'S at the same target: one
# statement flows into `$.t` outside any disjunction, and the
# alternative that survives inside the disjunction adds to it. Both
# reach the target, which is the same rule two plain refers follow
# (flow-two-refers above) with one of them inside a disjunction.
flow-survivor-merges-with-an-existing-record

column1: # A FLOW NESTED INSIDE ANOTHER ONE STILL REACHES ITS TARGET. Whichever
# link the evaluator happened to reach first once decided what the model
# said, so the same document accepted or refused depending on the order
# its statements were written in (BUGS.md 69). Each round of the
# evaluation meets every template the last round's output holds at its
# target, so the order decides nothing.
# Here `a.r` flows {v:1} into `$.b`, whose own `v` is 2. Unsatisfiable,
# and refused whichever of `a` and `c` is written first.
flow-nested-in-another-flow-still-lands
flow-nested-in-another-flow-order-does-not-decide
# The same shape where the nested flow is SATISFIABLE: it lands, and
# the target carries both types whichever order they are written in.
flow-nested-in-another-flow-lands-both-ways
# Integrity is a UNIFICATION-time property, not a vet-time one. Within
# one evaluation the document-set is fixed, so existence IS decidable:
# the target is looked for once the document is evaluated, so a node a
# later conjunct, include, spread or another link's template brings
# counts, as `link-forward` shows. A relative address that climbs off
# the top of the tree is the one shape refused AT ONCE: nothing can grow
# a tree upwards.
unresolved-node
unresolved-node-msg
unresolved-inside-a-node
unresolved-empty-document
# An ADDRESS-LESS relate is DONE, as `string` and `min(1)` are, and as
# `relate()` has been since it was written. It has nothing to check yet
# and nothing to refuse; the meet re-activates it the moment a value
# arrives, because map merges build the conjunct regardless.
# It used to be not-done, which cost the whole SCHEMA idiom
# (aontu-lang/aontu#172): a type() body holding a link never settled,
# so its mark never transferred, so generation could not skip the
# marked subtree and raised `mapval_no_gen` naming the DEFINITION -- a
# path that mentions neither the link nor the field. `type({p:
# integer})`, `type({p: path})` and `type({p: min(1)})` all settled;
# only a link did not. G4 phase 4 recorded the cost against
# `type({from: relate($.aontu.System.Port)})`, which the last three rows here are.
schema-type-body-holds-a-link
schema-type-body-link-canons
schema-closed-type-body-holds-a-link

# A PATH-DEPENDENT template is cloned per destination, so the residual
# it carries -- the type to flow, the address it has met -- has to
# travel with the clone. A constant template is SHARED, which is why
# only this shape reaches the clone path.
spread-path-dependent-template
# Two constraints held on ONE relate, accumulated into each other rather
# than replacing: both still meet the link when the address arrives.
held-two-constraints
held-two-constraints-refused
# THE FLOWED TYPE IS CONCRETE AT THE TARGET. A schema flowing into a
# value must not make the value a schema -- the same reasoning as a
# reference's clone clearing marks: `relate(type(t))` says the target IS
# a t, not that it is the definition of one. Without the clearing the
# target silently stopped generating. The marks are cleared on a COPY,
# `t` being shared by every position that refers to the same thing --
# and only when there are marks to clear, because cloning an unmarked
# type would move the site an error names.
flow-type-mark-cleared
flow-hide-mark-cleared
# A TYPED relate IN BOTH DIRECTIONS (use-cases/BUGS.md §19). The flow
# unifies `t` into the target, and uniting a target drives the target's
# own subtree -- so a pair that links back at each other used to flow
# into each other until the depth budget ended it, reporting
# unify_cycle on a model whose meet is a fixpoint on sight
# ({kind:service} meeting {kind:service}). Every inverse relation pair
# has this shape, so typing both ends was inexpressible and use case 01
# shipped the asymmetric workaround. Each template now meets its target
# as part of the document, once the document is evaluated, so a pair
# linked at each other is a fixpoint like any other meet, as the
# differs-each-way and cycle-of-three rows show. Parity-probed.
refer-typed-inverse-pair
